goal.what: The developers build and change the parts of the product so that together they deliver what the README promises the users.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know what each part must do, for the users or for the product's development and operation, and why.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the opening state the one idea by which the product delivers what its README promises?
necessary_conditions.why: Each part is a piece of one idea, and a developer who knows the idea builds a part that serves it.

items.text: Open your cut, and read to its end each input it names: the product vision, the README, and, where the product builds on another's rules, the architecture it builds on, such as a guide to building a plugin of the host it runs in.

In the README's How it works, take the first way it states, from the product vision's concept, by which the product brings its users to their objectives, such as keeping every decision of a run in one file that each role reads.
Ask how the system as a whole makes that way work: what it takes in from the roles, and what it turns that into, such as a request typed in a session turned into a deliverable that passed its checks.
Write the answer in two or three sentences that a developer can hold in mind while building any part. Point to the README instead of repeating it.

After writing the rest, read each component's line as a developer who knows only the idea, and check that they can see which piece of the idea it carries out. Change the idea or the component where they can't.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each step of each objective's main use, as the README's walkthrough shows it, have one user story that carries it?
necessary_conditions.why: The stories connect the parts to what the users do, so every part can trace back to a step a user takes. Jeff Patton's user story mapping lays the steps of the main use along a backbone, and hangs a [user story](https://www.mountaingoatsoftware.com/agile/user-stories) on each.

items.text: Open the README's walkthrough, and lay its exchanges in order as the backbone of the objective whose use it runs.

For each other objective of the product vision, lay as its backbone the steps its role takes from where they start to the result they keep, as a recorded run of that use shows them: a file that holds each step of one real run in order, what the role gave and what the product gave back, such as an end-to-end test's record or the files that a run of the product left in its folder. Search the repository's tests and each folder that the README says a run writes for one that ran that objective's use, and take none that ran another use. Where the search finds none, ask the user `Which steps does <role> take toward <objective>, from <start> to <result>?`, with the steps you'd expect as your recommendation, since only whoever conceived the product knows a use that no run shows.
For each step of each backbone, ask how the role meets the product at its edge there, such as a command they type, and write one story for each such way, naming the steps it carries.

Read each idea of the product vision's Concept, and ask at which moment of the use it keeps the product's one way holding. Where the role meets the product there in a way that no story carries, add a story for it, such as resuming a run that stopped, for an idea that keeps every decision of a run in one file.
Go through each step of each backbone, and name the one story that carries it. Add a story where none does.

necessary_conditions.about: Principles, User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each principle, user story, component, and kind of data trace to what the README promises the users, or to a need of the product's development or operation?
necessary_conditions.why: A part that nothing needs costs effort to build and to keep, and gives no one anything.

items.text: For each story, ask which step, doubt, or need it carries, from three sources. The README and the product vision carry what the users get: the steps of each backbone that N2 lays out, and the doubts that the README's How it works answers. Development adds what the developers need to build, test, and change the parts. Operation adds what keeps the product working across runs and updates, such as where its work outlives a run.
Once you have written Principles, for each principle, name the doubt of the README's How it works, or the need of development or operation, that it carries.
Once you have drawn Sequences, for each component and each kind of data, find the principle or the step of a sequence that reaches it.
Remove each story or principle that carries none, and each component or kind of data that none reaches, from every figure, list, and sentence that names it.

critical_success_factors.what: Parts that different developers build fit together.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each principle give a rule and a reason from which two developers decide a case that no line names the same way?
necessary_conditions.why: Developers of different parts meet the same kind of decision, and decide it apart unless a principle settles it.

items.text: Derive the principles from the README's How it works, which answers each doubt of the users from an idea of the product vision's concept, and from the needs of development and operation.

For each answer and each need, ask what every part must hold alike for it to come true, such as where the work's state lives. A part that held it otherwise would break a key result. Each thing that every part must hold alike is a principle.
Leave out what a single component's line already says, since a principle holds only a rule that spans parts.
For each principle, write the rule in one sentence, naming the parts as Components names them.

Write the reason in one sentence: what goes wrong without the rule, for a role of the product vision, naming the key result it guards, or for the developers or the operators. A developer carries the reason to a case that the rule doesn't name.
Where your cut names an architecture that the product builds on, point to its principles, and write only what this product adds or changes.

Take a case that no rule names from a step of a story where two components meet, such as a hook that finds the file of the work's state missing, and decide it from each reason as two developers of those two components would. Where they differ, sharpen the reason. For example, a rule that the work's state lives in one file says nothing of a missing file, and its reason, that every role reads the same decisions, decides that the hook stops the step rather than make a new file.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each decision that the stories need belong to exactly one component?
necessary_conditions.why: Two components that make the same decision make it twice, and the two copies drift apart. David Parnas's information hiding gives each module one decision that's hard to make or likely to change, and hides it from the rest.

items.text: Walk each story's steps, and name who acts at each: the role, a part of the product, or a thing outside the product. Each part of the product that acts is a component, of a kind that the architecture the product builds on offers where it offers kinds, such as a skill, a hook, or a script of a Claude Code plugin.
Take from the stories the decisions that are hard to make or likely to change, such as where the product keeps the work's state, or the form of a file that two parts share.

Give each decision to the one component that holds what it decides on, such as the form of the work's state to the component that writes the state. Where no component holds it, make a component for it.

Where another component needs the same decision, leave it with the component that holds it, and draw an arrow by which the other asks it, such as a hook that asks a script whether a step is done instead of reading the state itself.
List under the figure what each component alone decides.
Label each arrow with what one component does to another and the data it passes, not a word such as `uses`.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component state its type and its technology?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doesn't know what kind of thing a component is, or what it's built with, chooses alone, and the components stop fitting. The [C4 model](https://c4model.com/diagrams/container) gives each box its name, its type, such as a script, a skill, or a folder of JSON files, and its technology.

items.text: For each component, decide the type and the technology from the product's constraints, such as the runtime its users have.
Copy the template's skeleton of the figure to the deliverable's own, and place the boxes in the order the main story reaches them, left to right, so that its arrows run one way and cross no other.
Draw a store of data as a box like a component's, since its type sets it apart.
Give the figure a legend for every symbol.
Read the figure without the text around it, and add to the legend whatever symbol a reader would still have to ask about.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the data model show how each kind of data relates to the others, without its fields?
necessary_conditions.why: Two developers who build the writer and the reader of the same data must join it to the other data in the same way, while its fields stay free to change. A concept model in a class diagram of the Unified Modeling Language (UML), which most developers read, shows this.

items.text: Walk each story's steps and each arrow that Components draws, and list each kind of data that one component hands to another or that a store keeps, by the name the README gives it where it gives one, such as a run's record.
For each pair that relates, name the relation, and give how many of each it joins at both ends, such as a run that holds one or more rounds.
Draw each once, as a class by its name alone.
Where one holds the other's parts, put a filled diamond at the whole, since readers take a hollow one in different ways.
Group the data in a frame for each component or store that keeps them, in the order the stories meet them, with the data that most others join in the middle.
Leave the fields to where the developer builds the data.
Below the figure, say in a few words what a kind of data is only where a reader could take its name for another's.

necessary_conditions.about: User stories, Components, Data model, Sequences
necessary_conditions.what: Does each user story have a sequence that shows, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow, and with which data?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer building a step must know who acts there, on what, and what comes next. A [UML](https://www.omg.org/spec/UML) sequence diagram draws a story's steps in order, from the role's first request to what the story gives them.

items.text: For each story, draw each step as a message from one component to another along an arrow of Components, with the data it passes, named as in the data model.

At each step, ask what can go otherwise there, from the README's walkthrough and from what each component alone decides: an input that a component refuses, a check that fails, or a choice that only the role can make, such as a question that the walkthrough shows the role answering.

Draw an input refused as a branch, a check that fails as a step that sends work back to the step it repeats, and a choice of the role as a question put to the role with its answers, since each path of the story, and its integration test, rests on them.
Let stories that share their steps share a diagram.

Read each sequence as the developer who builds one of its steps, and check that they can tell, at each step, which component acts, along which arrow of Components, with which data, and what comes next. Where no arrow carries a step, add the arrow, or give the step to another component.

necessary_conditions.what: Do the figures, lists, and sentences agree with one another, and with the architecture that the product builds on, on what each part does?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who finds two places that say different things about a part must choose which to follow, and two developers choose differently.

items.text: For each part, gather what every figure, list, and sentence says it does, and, where your cut names an architecture that the product builds on, what each of its rules asks of a part of that kind, such as a rule that every hook gives its result as JSON.
Where two disagree, decide by the reasons of the principles and of those rules which is right, and change the other.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can place, set up, and start every part without asking anyone.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Deployment show where each component runs, where the product keeps each kind of data, and how the product starts?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer setting up the product needs to know where each part runs, what it can reach, and how it starts. A [C4 deployment diagram](https://c4model.com/diagrams/deployment) shows this.

items.text: List each environment the product runs in, such as the user's computer or CI, with its technology.
Place each component and each kind of data in one deployment unit within its environment, such as the plugin's folder that the host installs, or the run's folder in the user's repository.
Add each thing outside the product that the components depend on, with what they use of it, and no infrastructure that they don't need.
Write in one sentence how the product starts.
Check that a developer could set the product up from nothing by the figure and that sentence.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each component and each kind of data have one place for its files?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer making a change must find the one place it belongs. Simon Brown's package by component, in Robert C. Martin's *Clean Architecture*, lays out the code by the components that the architecture draws.

items.text: Lay out the folders by component, so that each component and each kind of data has its own place, such as a folder for the hooks and one for the code they call.

Once Test strategy names its levels and tools, give the test code its place, as a component's tests are files that a developer changes with it: one folder for each level, and the script that checks the trace beside them. Take the folder where the repository already keeps its tests, else the one where the architecture that the product builds on keeps them, else the one where the test runner that Test strategy names looks by default, such as `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/`, and `tests/e2e/` for pytest. Keep the test code out of every folder that the users install, and each level in a folder of its own, since each level runs at its own time and a command that runs one level names its folder.
Say in one sentence for each top folder whom its files are for, such as the users who install the product or only its developers.

Show each folder and file that holds a component, a kind of data, a level's test cases, or the script that checks the trace, by its real name, one line each, nested as on disk, without the files inside a component or a level's folder.
Beside each, say what it does or holds, in the words a developer looks for when making a change.
Check that, for any change to a component, a developer can name the one folder it goes in.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers find each gap between the parts before they build any part, and know, as they build, that the product does what the document and the product vision say.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Test strategy decide the types of testing of each target, every type of code and test quality for the parts and those the key results call for in the product vision's, and, for each test level, what it tests, what runs real, its tools, when it runs, and each quality check with the criterion by which it passes?
necessary_conditions.why: A case's pass or fail decides the work only where the developers set its level's tools and criteria before anyone writes the case, and a failure that no type of testing looks for reaches the users unseen.

items.text: Name the levels unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end (E2E) tests, and use no other name for a test. Unit tests try each part, each prompt among them, against its contract. Integration tests try the parts joined against each element of this document. E2E tests try the product in real use against each key result of the product vision.

For each level, run real only what it tests, and replace the rest with [test doubles](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDouble.html). At unit, run the part, with a double for each part it works with that's slow or outside the test. At integration, run what joins the components, such as hooks and scripts, with a double for each component that an AI runs and for each thing outside the product, so that the level calls no model and gives the same result on each run. At E2E, run the whole product on the model its users run, with an AI in the role that holds an intent the product never receives, since another model makes other mistakes than the users meet.
Read [the list of test types](test-types.md) to its end.

For the parts, take every type that the list gives under code quality and test quality, and, for each part that holds a prompt, every type under a prompt's evaluation, since each looks at every part alike, and a fault that one of them would show costs a key result wherever it lands.

Set the criterion of each type that the parts took. Take it from the architecture that the product builds on where that sets one. Else take the strictest that every part can meet once each line answers a case one level up: every line and branch covered, no mutant left alive, the default limits of the complexity and lint tools, and no finding of static analysis or lint. Where a line can't meet it, mark the line with why, since a check without a criterion passes whatever it finds.

Name each contract that takes a wide input, one that another program or an AI writes, such as the reader of a file that an AI writes, for property-based tests that find no counterexample, and leave the other contracts to the cases drawn by hand.

Set k, how many times a prompt's unit tests run each case on the model its users run, passing a case only where all k runs pass, as pass^k measures it, which Anthropic's [demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) takes from [τ-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045) for an agent whose users expect it to act right every time. Set k to the number of times one main use of an objective runs the prompt at the size of a real request, as the backbones that N2 lays out show it, such as 5 for a prompt run once for each of five deliverables, since a slip in any of those runs costs that use its key result. Where no backbone shows how many times, ask the user `How many times does <prompt> run in one use toward <objective> at its real size?`, with your count as your recommendation.

Set the quality checks of the architecture, and name the script that checks them by the names of the elements, not by reading: every element of this document, each story, principle, component, and kind of data, has an integration test; every test names an element or a case one level up that exists; every unit case names an integration case; a test of a principle that must not break is trusted only once seen to fail with the principle broken; and each double gives only what a recorded run or the official documentation shows, as N14 says.

For each key result of the product vision, ask of each type that the parts didn't take whether, without it, the key result could worsen and no check would show it, given what the product is and what it builds on, such as compatibility with a new version of the host where the host changes on its own schedule. Keep each type where it could, and drop the rest, since testing every type that could apply is the trivial many. Leave out functional testing, which every level's cases try, as N13 says.
For each type kept, write the key result it guards as its reason, and the lowest level at which what it looks at runs real, such as E2E for the time a main use takes.
Set the criterion of each type kept only as far as the failure it guards calls for, such as no main use slower than in the last run, in place of a fixed time that no key result asks for.

Where you keep compatibility with a new version of what the product builds on, set its check at the integration level, whose doubles it keeps true: on each new version of the thing outside the product, run again the steps that made each recorded run, and compare what the real thing gives with what each double gives, passing only where they agree. This is Martin Fowler's [contract test](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ContractTest.html), which runs against the real thing apart from the work.
Where a double rests on a page of documentation and not on a recorded run, add to that check that the page still shows the words the double rests on.

Decide what the developers do where that check fails: record the new version's run, change the double to give what the run shows, and fix the product where a test then fails, since a double that the real thing has outgrown passes a test that its users' version fails.
Set the check of each key result: compare its value with the last run's by the order the product vision gives, and pass where it's no worse, since the product vision sets no target.
Where an AI judges a key result, trust the judge only once it's right on every kept record whose answer you know.

Set how many times each E2E test runs its main use at real size by its first runs: run the main use on the product, and add runs until one more no longer moves the mean of each key result by a step of its measure, such as one question answered, since the AI's variance shows only across runs, and a mean that one more run would move can't tell a change from noise. Where the product can't run its main use yet, write this rule in place of the number, for the first E2E run to set it.
Choose each level's tools from the product's constraints, such as the runtime its users have, and name each: the test runner, and the tool of each check, such as pytest for a product in Python.

Run before each push the static analysis, the unit tests of code, and the integration tests that the change reaches, with their coverage, since these show whether the change does what its design says, and the work waits on them. Running every such test there meets this too, as a selection by what the change reaches misses a test that reads a file the change edits.

Run on each push, in CI, every unit test of code and every integration test, and mutation testing and property-based tests over the lines that the push changed, apart from the work, since these check the tests and not the change.

Run each night, in CI, every check that runs on its own over the whole, property-based tests at their most inputs among them, since a run over a push's lines misses a test changed alone and a fault between parts that no one push changed together.

Run the compatibility check of each double on each new version of the thing outside the product, which a job in CI finds each night by its version, since only a new version changes what the double must give.
Run a prompt's unit tests before a change of the prompt is taken, since each run calls the model and is slow and costly.
Run the E2E tests once every lower level passes, since each run calls the model and is slow and costly.
Write a subsection for each level, from unit to E2E, in the form of the template.
Where your cut names an architecture that the product builds on, point to its test rules, such as the form each case takes, and write only what this product sets.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each part have its skeleton, and every part, every element of this document, and every key result its test cases in the test code, each written as Given, When, and Then through that skeleton, and each naming the case or the element one level up that it supports?
necessary_conditions.why: Every case written through a skeleton of the parts before any body is built checks the architecture while a gap between the parts is still cheap to fix: a case that no part can hold, or a handoff that no interface carries, shows the gap before anyone builds around it. Steve Freeman and Nat Pryce's outside-in test-driven development, in [Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests](http://www.growing-object-oriented-software.com/) and [Mock Roles, not Objects](http://jmock.org/oopsla2004.pdf), finds each part's roles and interface by first writing the tests one level up. A case finds a gap only where it calls a real interface, and the skeleton is code, apart from this document, which keeps no part's internals.

items.text: Once Test strategy names the tools, make the skeleton of each module where Directory structure places it, from the arrows and the data that Sequences hand to it: a file whose docstring names the decision it alone makes, and, for each arrow it takes, an interface whose signature and docstring state what it takes, what it gives, and what it refuses, each body left empty, such as one that raises `NotImplementedError`.

Where a part holds a prompt, make its skeleton where Directory structure places it: a file with its description, which says when to use the prompt and what it gives, and the form of what it takes and gives, such as a JSON Schema, its steps left empty.

Write the E2E cases first: for each key result, a case that runs an objective's main use, as the README's walkthrough shows it, at the size of a real request, and names the key result, such as `KR1.1`.

Write the integration cases from the elements of this document, each naming its element by its name: a case for each path through each story's sequence, the main flow, each branch, each step that sends work back, and each question put to the role, until every move from one step to the next lies on some path; a case for each principle, where the parts keep it and where one breaks it; a case for each decision that a component alone makes; and a case for each handoff between parts, with the data it passes as the data model names it, until each kind of data lies on some case.

Write the unit cases of each part through its interface, each naming the integration case it supports, so that the interface a part offers comes from what the cases one level up need of it, and change the skeleton where a case needs an interface it lacks or calls none it offers.

Divide each input and each result that a part's contract names into classes that the part treats alike, the refused ones among them, and write one case for each class. This is equivalence partitioning, as the ISTQB glossary defines it.
Where a class ends on an ordered scale, such as a length or a count, write one case at each end and one at the nearest value of the next class. This is boundary value analysis.
Where the contract's result depends on a combination of conditions, write one case for each combination that can occur, with the result it gives. This is decision table testing.

For a prompt, write a case where its contract says it acts and one where it says it doesn't, for each kind of request it's for, and decide by code each point of the result that the record of each of its runs on the model shows: each tool call the prompt's AI made, each message it gave, and each file at the run's end, such as the JSON it passed to a script, since an AI that judged them would vary from run to run.

Write each case as a test in the test code, in the folder of its level that Directory structure names, with its Given, When, and Then stated, and write no list of the cases in a document, since a list beside the code says each case twice.

Run the type checker over the skeleton and the cases, and see every case fail: a type that doesn't fit across a handoff is a gap between the parts, and a case that passes on an empty body tests nothing.

Read the cases and the skeleton against the architecture, and list each gap they show: a case that no part can hold; a part that no case reaches; a module that can't state its decision in a few words; a part whose cases change for more than one reason, such as a file's form and a remote's commands; and a handoff that no interface carries.

For each gap, change the architecture first: give the case a part, or a decision to a part; remove the part that no case reaches, as N3 says; split the module or the part by its decisions or its reasons to change; and give the handoff an arrow and a kind of data.
Then change the skeleton and the cases to the architecture.

Make the script that checks the trace, which N12.8 names, beside the test code where Directory structure places it, so that it finds each element by where the template puts its name, such as each story by its `S<n>` and each key result by its `KR<n>.<m>`, finds each case by the name it gives of what it supports, and checks each rule that N12.8 sets. Where the architecture the product builds on keeps such a script, such as one that a guide to building plugins runs on every plugin, run that one on this product instead, and add only the checks it lacks.

Run the script that checks the trace, and mend each case or element it names until it names none. The script finds only a name that leads nowhere, so its 0 shows no more than that: whether the cases are enough, and whether the parts are cut right, the reading before it judges.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each thing that the document says the product does rest on a part that a unit or integration test can check?
necessary_conditions.why: The E2E tests are slow and few, so they can only confirm what the lower levels already showed, and a thing that only a prompt holds varies from run to run, where only many runs on the model show it. The [Humble Object](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/HumbleObject.html) pattern of Gerard Meszaros's *xUnit Test Patterns* moves the logic out of a part that's hard to test into a part that a test can run.

items.text: List each thing the product does, as the README's walkthrough and How it works say it and as your decisions so far give it: each step that a story carries, each principle, and each decision that a component alone makes. For each, name the part that holds it, such as the script that writes the file of the work's state for keeping every decision of a run in one file.
Where only a prompt holds a rule that must hold on every run, give the rule to a part that a test can run, such as a guard of the architecture the product builds on, and draw that part in Components.
Leave a judgment that only an AI can make, such as whether a point is the user's, with the AI, and try it by the prompt's unit tests on the model, as N12.7 sets.
The lower levels show a part only if each double behaves like the part it replaces, so give each double only results in the form the part's contract gives, refusals among them.
Test each double as the part's unit tests test the part.

For each result that a double of something outside the product gives, find what shows the real thing giving it: a page of its documentation that says so, or a recorded run, a file that holds each input the real thing got and each result it gave in one run, named by the thing and its version, such as `claude-code-2.1.322.jsonl` with each hook event that a run of Claude Code 2.1.322 sent. Look for recorded runs where the architecture the product builds on says it keeps them, and else among the test code. Where neither shows the result, run the real thing on the steps that give it and keep each input and result in such a file. Where you can't run it, such as a service you have no account for, ask the user `Can you record a run of <thing> that gives <result>?`.

Draw each double's results from that source alone, and name the source beside what the double gives, so that the script that N13.15 makes to check the trace can check it. A double that gives what the real thing never would passes a test that the real one fails.

For each check, such as a test of a principle or a hook, write a case that breaks what it checks, such as the principle's test with the part that holds the principle taken out, and make the script that N13.15 makes to check the trace run the check on that case and fail where the check passes there, since a check never seen to fail may pass whatever it meets. Every case fails while the bodies are empty, so the run shows a check failing for the break alone only once a developer builds the part's body: write the case and the script now, and leave that run to the developer's push.

Leave the trial of each E2E test's judge to the first E2E runs, since they keep the first records: the maintainer, when asked, gives the answer of each record they keep, and the developers trust the judge, as N12.16 sets, once it gives every such answer.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can change the product without making the document wrong.

necessary_conditions.about: Components, Deployment, Directory structure, Test strategy
necessary_conditions.what: Does each choice whose other way would cost a key result say what the other way would lose?
necessary_conditions.why: A developer who doubts a choice and can't see what it was for may undo it and bring back the problem it solved. An [architecture decision record](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), by Michael Nygard, keeps a decision with its context and consequences.

items.text: For each choice whose other way would bring back a problem that costs a key result, such as a technology, a tool, or the k of a prompt's unit tests, name the other way it beat, what the choice gives, ending with the key result it serves, and what it costs.
Write it beside the choice, one sentence for each.
For each choice that a figure shows, ask what the other way would bring back. Give a reason and a cost only where it would cost a key result.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the document hold only what stays true while the product vision and the principles stay, and leave each component's internals out?
necessary_conditions.why: A line about how a component works inside becomes untrue at the next change to that component, and the developer then can't trust the document. David Parnas's [information hiding](https://doi.org/10.1145/361598.361623) keeps such details inside the module.

items.text: For each line, ask whether it would become untrue if a component's internals changed while the product vision and the principles stayed.
If it would, move it to where the developer builds the component.

Imagine a change to how a component works inside, such as its steps, a value it uses, or a data's fields, and mark each line it would make untrue. Repeat with a change of another kind until you mark no line.
